findings.claim: Aggregate visitor arrivals look 'back to normal': 2025 is 10.01M vs 2024's 10.17M, a 1.6% YoY dip, which supports a surface narrative of recovery.
The flat aggregate is a Simpson's Paradox: Maui grew +3.75% YoY while Oahu fell -4.55%, with Hawaii and Kauai essentially flat. Oahu alone lost 240k visitors vs 2024.
findings.evidence: Computed from tourism_monthly.csv, groupby year x island.

findings.claim: Oahu is the only source of net decline. It accounts for 148% of the total YoY drop (i.e., the other three islands combined offset ~78k visitors of gains). Without Oahu's issue, the portfolio would be in modest net growth.
findings.evidence: Sum of per-island deltas compared to total delta.

findings.claim: Oahu's decline is accelerating within 2025, not stabilizing. Q1 ran -2 to -3% YoY; Q4 ran -7 to -9% YoY. October 2025 was -9.4%, the worst month in the dataset.
findings.evidence: Monthly Oahu YoY deltas, month-of-year 2025 vs 2024.

findings.claim: Oahu's decline concentrates in the hotel segment, which lost 160k visitors (67% of Oahu's total decline). Hotel-luxury alone lost 73k visitors (31% of Oahu's decline) at -10.1% YoY; hotel-mid_market lost 74k (31% of Oahu's decline) at -4.6% YoY.
findings.evidence: Oahu subset, groupby accommodation_type x tier.

findings.claim: Within Oahu hotel-luxury, US_mainland is the largest absolute loss (-42.5k, 58% of the hotel-luxury decline) but Japanese visitors dropped the steepest (-12.6% YoY, -16.5k). This isn't an Oahu-specific Japan issue generally; it's specifically Japan's taste for Oahu luxury hotels.
findings.evidence: Oahu hotel-luxury subset, groupby origin_market. Cross-checked against Japan-hotel-luxury across all islands: Oahu's -16.5k dominates a -15.9k total (other islands slightly positive).

findings.claim: A substitution effect is partially visible: Maui gained ~51k US_mainland visitors while Oahu lost ~157k US_mainland visitors. Maui's hotel-luxury grew +2.4% YoY across all origins. This looks like mainland travelers choosing Maui over Oahu - but it is not a net wash (Oahu's loss exceeds Maui's gain by roughly 3x).
findings.evidence: US_mainland by island: Maui +51k, Oahu -157k. Maui hotel-luxury +7.3k, Oahu hotel-luxury -73.4k.

findings.claim: Oahu's decline is concentrated - 77.7% of Oahu's total YoY loss comes from just 10 (accommodation x tier x origin) cells out of 45 possible cells, and 62% from the top 5. This means interventions can target a narrow set of segments, not the whole island's tourism stack.
findings.evidence: Ranked Oahu cells by abs_delta; cumulative share of decline.

findings.claim: The decline is structural, not seasonal. H1 2025 Oahu ran -2.7% YoY; H2 2025 ran -6.3% YoY. Peak months (June/July/August, December) are still the peaks - the shape is intact, but the level is depressed, and the gap is widening in Q4.
findings.evidence: H1/H2 YoY comparisons by island; month-over-month pattern shape preserved but trend drops.

hypothesis_results.H1: supported - Simpson's Paradox confirmed; aggregate -1.6% hides -4.6% Oahu and +3.8% Maui
hypothesis_results.H2: supported - Oahu is the sole net-decline island; other three are flat or positive
hypothesis_results.H3: supported - Oahu decline concentrates in 10 of 45 cells (77.7%); hotel tier, luxury and mid-market drive most
hypothesis_results.H4: partially supported - origin-mix is uneven (Japan luxury-hotel is a notable outlier on Oahu specifically) but US_mainland is the dominant absolute driver due to volume
hypothesis_results.H5: supported - seasonal shape intact; decline is level not shape; H2 is deteriorating faster than H1
